\begin{abstract}
Whether a medical vision-language model (VLM) uses the image is commonly assessed by removing it: the
consistent-but-dangerous taxonomy labels an answer \dang{} when it is stable under paraphrase and unchanged
without the image. We test whether this criterion can rank models. Three medical VLMs and the general-purpose
models they were built from (MedGemma-4B and MedGemma-1.5-4B \vs Gemma-3-4B; MedVLThinker-3B \vs Qwen2.5-VL-3B)
answer the same yes/no questions on CT, MRI, X-ray and pathology images without the image and under three
\emph{in-format} probes that keep an image in the input: a different image, a black image, and an image for which
the same question has the opposite answer. By image removal, MedGemma-4B appears less image-reliant than
Gemma-3-4B (\dang{} share higher by 13.7 points\ci{10.0}{17.5}; pre-registered). Tested directly, as a difference
of differences on the same questions, image removal ranks a medical model against its base differently from an
in-format probe in 13 of 21 comparisons after Holm correction, in 6 of 9 model-pair~$\times$~dataset cells, and by
up to 60.5 points\ci{51.3}{68.8} against the opposite-answer image. The image-removal differences track refusal
(without an image, Gemma-3 declines on 29\% of questions, and its forced answers there are unrelated to its answers
with the image) and the agreement between a model's priors and the image. In-format probes have a confound of their
own: both MedGemma models follow opposite-answer images far more than Gemma-3 on SLAKE, which they were trained on
(+48.0 and +36.5 points), but not on held-out PathVQA (+0.8 and $-5.6$; registered before it was run), where every
model's result is within 6 points of what its accuracy alone predicts. Image removal should not be used to compare
image reliance between models; such comparisons require opposite-answer images on data outside each model's
training set, read against accuracy.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
A model that answers a question about an image without using the image is not performing visual question
answering, however accurate its answers. In general-domain VQA, this concern motivated balanced benchmarks and
prior-robust splits~\cite{goyal2017vqav2,agrawal2018dont}. Medical VQA is still evaluated predominantly by
accuracy, although the stakes are higher: an answer derived from language priors is most likely to fail on
exactly the patients whose images are atypical.

Neither accuracy nor consistency under rephrasing distinguishes using the image from guessing well; a model that
ignores the image can be \emph{more} consistent, since no visual signal perturbs it~\cite{sadanandan2026psfmed}.
Sadanandan and Behzadan~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} therefore combined the two criteria per answer. An
answer is \emph{consistent} if it is stable under paraphrase, and \emph{image-reliant} if it changes when the
image is removed. The resulting quadrants are \textsc{Ideal} (consistent, reliant), \textsc{Fragile},
\dang{} (consistent, not reliant) and \textsc{Worst}. On chest X-rays, they found that fine-tuning for
consistency moves most answers into \dang{}.

Such a taxonomy invites comparisons between models, and these comparisons are only as valid as the reliance
criterion. Removing the image changes the input format: a model asked about an absent image may decline, answer
from priors, or guess, and none of these responses is equivalent to ignoring an image that is present. For chest
radiography, Lotfinia~\etal~\cite{lotfinia2026cxr} accordingly treat performance without the image as a model's
default answer rather than as evidence of image use. Whether this matters for comparisons between models, which is
how a taxonomy is typically used, has not been tested. We therefore compare image removal with probes that keep an
image in the input, on the same questions, for three medical VLMs and the general-purpose models they were derived
from: MedGemma-4B~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma} and MedGemma-1.5-4B against Gemma-3-4B~\cite{gemma2025gemma3}, and
MedVLThinker-3B against Qwen2.5-VL-3B, on CT, MRI, X-ray and pathology questions from three public benchmarks.

We do not assume that any probe is the ground truth. The claim we test is narrower and does not need one: if two
probes measured the same property, they would order a pair of models the same way. \Cref{fig:bydataset} shows that
they do not. Image removal ranks a medical model against its base differently from the in-format probes in six of
nine model-pair~$\times$~dataset cells, and the probes agree only where the differences are small. Conversely,
the in-format probes indicate substantially greater image reliance for both MedGemma models only on SLAKE, a
dataset in their training data; on PathVQA, which none of the medical models was trained on, a pre-registered test
finds no such advantage, and what the probe reports there is close to what accuracy alone predicts.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Probes disagree about which model relies on the image.} Four reliance probes are run on identical
questions for three medical/general model pairs and three datasets, and their disagreement is tested directly. The
individual probes have precedent~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent,zafar2026see,lotfinia2026cxr}; to our knowledge,
their conclusions about the same models have not been compared.
\item \textbf{What image removal responds to.} Refusal under a forced yes/no format and agreement between a model's
prior and the image account for its differences; a chance floor and a decomposition by correctness show what the
\dang{} share contains.
\item \textbf{What in-format probes respond to.} A pre-registered held-out test shows that the in-format advantage
of two medical models on their training distribution does not transfer, and that the opposite-answer probe largely
reports competence on the evaluated distribution.
\end{itemize}
The pipeline, manifests, registrations and all model outputs are public; every later probe and model pair was
registered before it was run.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}
\paragraph{Language priors and modality reliance.} Balanced pairs~\cite{goyal2017vqav2} and changing-prior
splits~\cite{agrawal2018dont} showed that general VQA models exploit answer priors. MMStar~\cite{chen2024mmstar}
measures the gain from the image and the leakage of benchmark items into training data, the general-domain
counterpart of the exposure we test with held-out data. MM-SHAP~\cite{parcalabescu2023mmshap} and the perceptual
score~\cite{gat2021perceptual} quantify modality contributions by masking or permuting inputs. Contrast
sets~\cite{gardner2020contrast} and NaturalBench~\cite{li2024naturalbench} score inputs with different answers
jointly, which a model that ignores the image cannot pass; our pair accuracy applies this to medical images.

\paragraph{Image use in medical VLMs.} PSF-Med~\cite{sadanandan2026psfmed} measured paraphrase flip rates across
medical VLMs on chest X-rays and noted that low flip rates frequently co-occur with high text-only agreement. The
quadrant taxonomy~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} defines reliance by image removal and corroborates it with a
KL-divergence score, a black image and random image swaps, which agreed with image removal on their models.
Zafar~\etal~\cite{zafar2026see} construct blank, pixel-shuffled, absent and CLIP-retrieved hard-negative images
to define reliance metrics and train a model against them. Lotfinia~\etal~\cite{lotfinia2026cxr} swap, occlude and
remove chest radiographs, take the opposite-label swap as the primary test because accuracy without the image
reflects a model's default answer and the label distribution, and find that model class (medical or general) does
not predict image use. ProbMed~\cite{yan2025probmed} pairs medical questions with adversarial counterparts and finds
large models below chance. Pathology VLMs reach high accuracy without the image~\cite{zhang2026pathology}, and
medical MLLMs frequently attend to irrelevant regions~\cite{liu2026medmllmfail}. Grounding inputs can even reduce
closed-ended accuracy~\cite{chen2026grounding}; HEAL-MedVQA~\cite{nguyen2025heal} and
MedHEval~\cite{chang2025medheval} benchmark localization and hallucination. These studies use a single probe, treat
several as interchangeable, or argue against removal on conceptual grounds; we measure how the conclusions of
different probes about the same models diverge, explain the divergence, and test it inside and outside the models'
training data.

\paragraph{Answering without evidence.} MedVIGIL~\cite{jiang2026medvigil} tests whether models abstain when
visual evidence is corrupted, and Vohra~\cite{vohra2026hearsay} reports that frontier VLMs produce diagnoses for
images that were never provided, and attaching even a blank image shifts refusal behavior~\cite{zhang2026uncontrolled},
so neither an absent nor a blank image is a neutral control. Four of our five open models decline almost always
when permitted to; we show how enforcing an answer affects a reliance criterion.

\paragraph{Selective prediction.} Ranking answers by a score and abstaining on the lowest-ranked ones is evaluated
by AUROC and risk--coverage~\cite{geifman2017selective}; we use this framework to test whether image reliance
identifies errors.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}
\subsection{Data}
\textbf{SLAKE}~\cite{liu2021slake} (English; CT, MRI, X-ray; 2,114 test and validation questions; the only
dataset with modality labels, with the validation split included so that each modality has 53--82 images).
\textbf{VQA-RAD}~\cite{lau2018vqarad} (radiology, clinician-written; all 451 test questions from the original
release). \textbf{PathVQA}~\cite{he2020pathvqa} (pathology, generated from textbook captions; 600 yes/no and 200
open test questions sampled with a fixed seed). In total, the main run covers 3,365 questions on 907 images. A
question is yes/no if its reference answer is \emph{yes} or \emph{no}. The \textbf{primary analysis set} comprises
the 1,206 yes/no \emph{test} questions on 670 images. The held-out opposite-answer probe uses a separate set: all
1,192 PathVQA test and validation yes/no questions that are also asked of another image with the opposite answer
(682 images). Sampling, partner images and image hashes are fixed in committed manifests, so that every run
receives identical inputs.

\subsection{Models}
\textbf{MedGemma-4B} (\texttt{google/medgemma-4b-it}) is an open medical VLM whose SigLIP-based
encoder~\cite{zhai2023siglip} and language model were further trained on medical data. Its technical
report~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma} lists SLAKE (450 items, the size of SLAKE's training split) and VQA-RAD
(reinforcement-learning stage) among its training data and states that PathVQA was excluded.
\textbf{Gemma-3-4B} (\texttt{google/gemma-3-4b-it}) has the same architecture and size. \textbf{MedGemma-1.5-4B}
(\texttt{google/medgemma-1.5-4b-it}, released in 2026; its model card lists SLAKE) is compared with the same
Gemma-3-4B, and \textbf{MedVLThinker-3B} (\texttt{UCSC-VLAA/MedVLThinker-3B-RL\_PMC}, Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct
trained with reinforcement learning on PMC-VQA) with its base model \textbf{Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct}. A medical
model and its base differ in their entire post-training, not only in medical data; we therefore compare
\emph{checkpoints} rather than attribute differences to medical training as such. All five models run unquantized
in bf16 on a single 16\,GB GPU, since quantization would perturb the probabilities under study, and receive
identical prompts: a fixed system message, the question, and ``Answer with only `yes' or `no'.'' or ``Answer with
a single word or short phrase.'' Each model added after the primary pair passed a registered format check
(mean first-token yes/no probability mass with the image $\ge0.9$ in every dataset of a 330-question pilot;
observed 0.93--0.999).

\subsection{Probes}
\label{sec:probes}
Each question is posed with its own image (\textbf{orig}) and as screened paraphrases with the same image
(\cref{sec:para}). Image reliance is probed by altering only the image or the instruction:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Image removed}: image tokens omitted, text unchanged; the reliance criterion of the
taxonomy~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent}.
\item \textbf{Different image} (``wrong image'' in the figures): another image from the same dataset and
modality, selected by a hash of the question identifier.
\item \textbf{Black image}: a black image in place of the original, preserving the input format but removing the
content.
\item \textbf{Opposite-answer image}: another image of the same dataset and modality for which the \emph{same}
question has the opposite reference answer; a model that uses the image must change its answer. Such partners exist
for 367 SLAKE yes/no questions (130 images), whose templated questions recur across images, and for the 1,192
held-out PathVQA questions above.
\item \textbf{Abstention permitted}: image removed, with the instruction extended by ``If this cannot be
determined without seeing the image, answer `unknown'.'' This probe measures refusal, not reliance.
\end{itemize}
We refer to the different-image, black-image and opposite-answer probes as \emph{in-format} probes, since an image
is present in the input.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\caption{What each probe can show. ``Fixed'': an image-reliant model has exactly one admissible response. The last
column lists the confound we observe (\cref{sec:what,sec:r4}).}
\label{tab:validity}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.23\linewidth}ccp{0.49\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Probe & Image & Fixed & Responds also to\\
\midrule
Image removed & no & no & refusal; agreement between prior and image\\
Different image & yes & no & nothing, when the partner image has the same answer\\
Black image & yes & no & how a model reads an empty image\\
Opposite-answer image & yes & yes & competence on the evaluated distribution, hence training exposure\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{No probe is the ground truth.} \Cref{tab:validity} summarizes what each probe can and cannot show. Only
the opposite-answer image fixes what an image-reliant model must do, namely change its answer, and change it to the
correct one; a black image is not a neutral input~\cite{zhang2026uncontrolled}, and a random image often has the
same correct answer. We therefore use the opposite-answer probe as the \emph{reference} where it exists, on SLAKE
and PathVQA. VQA-RAD has too few recurring questions for it, so comparisons there rest on the two weaker in-format
probes, and we say so where it matters. Image removal and the different image belong to the pre-registered main
run; the remaining probes and the two additional model pairs were each registered after the results that motivated
them and before they were run (identifiers in \cref{app:ids}).

\subsection{Measures}
\textbf{Yes/no answers} are obtained from a single forward pass,
$P(\text{yes})=\sigma(\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in Y}\,\ell_t-\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in N}\,\ell_t)$, over the single-token
variants of \emph{yes} and \emph{no}; the first-token mass $m=P(Y)+P(N)$ is recorded as a format check.
\textbf{Open answers} are decoded greedily and scored by token-F1$\,\ge0.5$ after normalization, with a guard that
prevents opposite terms (left/right, upper/lower, \etc) from matching. An answer is \textbf{consistent} if the
answers to the first two valid paraphrases equal the \emph{orig} answer, and \textbf{reliant} under a probe if the
probe answer differs from the \emph{orig} answer. The share of reliant answers is the \textbf{answer-change rate}
of that probe; it is the measure on which we compare probes, and the medical $-$ general difference in it is our
headline quantity. The \textbf{quadrant} follows from (consistent, reliant), and the \dang{} share is the
taxonomy's summary of it. \textbf{Refusal} is $m<0.5$, \ie the majority of first-token mass falls on neither
\emph{yes} nor \emph{no}; free generation confirms that these responses are requests for the image
(\cref{fig:teaser}a). The \textbf{image PMI} of an answer $\hat y$ is
$\log p(\hat y\mid I,q)-\log p(\hat y\mid\varnothing,q)$.

\paragraph{Opposite-answer pairs.} Because the two reference answers are opposite, a model that changes its answer
is right on both images or wrong on both, and a model that keeps its answer is right on exactly one. \textbf{Pair
accuracy} is the share of pairs answered correctly on both images~\cite{gardner2020contrast}. It has two reference
points: 0\% for a model that ignores the image, by construction, and 25\% for a model whose answers depend on the
image but carry no information. Accuracy over the two images decomposes exactly into pair accuracy plus half the
share of unchanged answers, so the second term is the part of a model's accuracy that does not come from the image.
As a summary, we compare pair accuracy with the product of the two single-image accuracies, which is what it would
be if being right on one image said nothing about the other.

\paragraph{Chance correction.} Cohen's $\kappa$~\cite{cohen1960kappa} between \emph{orig} and probe answers
corrects for chance agreement; the \emph{chance floor} of the \dang{} share is $P(\text{consistent})\cdot p_e$,
where $p_e$ is the agreement expected from the two answer distributions alone.

\subsection{Paraphrase construction and screening}
\label{sec:para}
Paraphrase consistency is meaningful only if a paraphrase cannot change the correct answer. Candidates are
generated by Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} (greedy decoding; five styles) and by two deterministic
templates that copy every content word (``Is there X?''$\to$``Is X present?''). A rule-based validator rejects
changes to laterality, negation and absence terms, quantities, antonyms, imaging planes, question form, answer
leakage, near-copies and length. Two audit rounds accepted 81\% and 83\% of sampled pairs, below the pre-specified
85\%; we therefore tightened the rules, excluded a ``plain language'' style, and \textbf{judged every unique
rule-valid (question, paraphrase) pair}, 4,890 in total, against a written rubric (\cref{app:rubric}). The judge
was an LLM (Claude); see \cref{sec:limits}. It rejected 1,208 pairs, each with a recorded reason (\eg
\emph{mass$\to$lesion}, \emph{is enlarged$\to$can be enlarged}); unjudged pairs are rejected by construction. Of
the primary-set questions, 84\% retain at least two valid paraphrases; quadrant analyses use these (1,012
questions, 600 images). The comparison between probes does not use paraphrases.

\subsection{Statistics and pre-registration}
Hypotheses, endpoints, tests and exclusions were fixed before the main run~\cite{nosek2018prereg}; every later
change is listed in \cref{app:dev}, and post-hoc analyses are identified as such. Because several questions share
an image, all intervals are percentile 95\% CIs from a cluster bootstrap over images~\cite{field2007bootstrap}
($B=2000$), with two-sided bootstrap $p$-values. Holm correction~\cite{holm1979} is applied within each family of
registered tests (\cref{tab:tests,app:ids}). A finding is considered robust only if its sign holds across a grid of
F1 thresholds (0.3/0.5/0.8), paraphrase counts (1/2/3) and ``strong'' flips.

\paragraph{Testing disagreement between probes.} That one probe finds a difference between two models and another
does not is not evidence that the probes disagree~\cite{gelman2006difference}. We therefore test the disagreement
itself. For a model pair, a dataset and an in-format probe, let $\Delta_{\text{removal}}$ and $\Delta_{\text{probe}}$
be the medical $-$ general differences in answer-change rate on the same questions; the statistic is
$\Delta_{\text{removal}}-\Delta_{\text{probe}}$, with a CI from the same bootstrap over images and Holm correction
over all 21 comparisons. This analysis is post hoc.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
All runs completed: 18,896 model calls per model in the main run, 3,535 for the three later probes and 2,384 for
the held-out opposite-answer probe, for each of the five models. The pipeline reproduces MedGemma's published SLAKE
score (token-F1 70.2\ci{67.5}{72.7} \vs 72.3 on the model card; Gemma-3: 45.1 \vs 40.2), and the yes/no format
mass with the image is $\ge0.997$ in every dataset. With the image, MedGemma-4B is more accurate than Gemma-3 on
yes/no questions by 18 points on SLAKE and 25 on VQA-RAD, both part of its training data, and by 2 points on
PathVQA, which is not (\cref{tab:acc}).

\subsection{What image removal reports}
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig1_quadrants.pdf}
\caption{Quadrant composition of yes/no answers (test split), MedGemma-4B and Gemma-3-4B. Left: reliance assessed
by removing the image (the taxonomy's definition). Right: by a different image of the same modality. Shares are
uncorrected; on yes/no questions they include chance agreement and correct answers (\cref{sec:what}).}
\label{fig:quad}
\end{figure*}

Under image removal, MedGemma-4B's \dang{} share is 50.6/46.8/56.5\% (PathVQA/SLAKE/VQA-RAD), compared with
43.2/28.1/31.0\% for Gemma-3 (\cref{fig:quad}, left). The paired difference of
\textbf{+13.7 points}\ci{10.0}{17.5} ($p<0.001$; 1,012 questions, 600 images) is positive in every dataset
(PathVQA +7.5\ci{2.6}{12.3}, SLAKE +18.6\ci{12.2}{24.9}, VQA-RAD +25.6\ci{14.7}{36.5}) and in every cell of the
sensitivity grid. MedGemma-1.5 shows the same pattern (+9.8\ci{5.8}{13.9}). The \dang{} share combines two
properties, and MedGemma-4B is also the more consistent model (paraphrase flip rate 6.8\% \vs 13.6\% on SLAKE). On
the reliance axis alone, which the remaining sections use, MedGemma-4B's answers change less often when the image
is removed ($-6.1$ points\ci{$-9.5$}{$-2.7$}, pooled over datasets). Taken at face value, the medical models more
often give stable answers that do not depend on the image.

\Cref{fig:bydataset} reports the medical $-$ general difference in answer-change rate under every probe, and
\cref{tab:did} tests whether image removal and each in-format probe report the same difference. They do not: the
difference of differences excludes zero in 13 of the 21 comparisons after Holm correction, covering six of the
nine pair~$\times$~dataset cells. Against the reference probe, the opposite-answer image on SLAKE, image removal is
off by 60.5 points\ci{51.3}{68.8} for MedGemma-4B and by 45.5\ci{34.0}{56.5} for MedGemma-1.5, and it has the
opposite sign: by image removal both models rely on the image less than Gemma-3, by the opposite-answer image far
more. On VQA-RAD, where no reference probe exists, image removal reports that both MedGemma models change their
answers about 19 points less often than Gemma-3 and that MedVLThinker changes them 11 points more often than its
base. Neither of the weaker in-format probes finds any of these differences, and the disagreement is significant in
all six comparisons.

The probes agree in three cells. For the Qwen pair on SLAKE, no probe finds a difference. For MedGemma-1.5 on
PathVQA, image removal ($-4.3$), a different image ($-6.0$) and the opposite-answer image ($-5.6$) point the same
way. For the Qwen pair on PathVQA, image removal reports a small difference (+4.5\ci{1.7}{7.2}) that the in-format
probes do not, but the disagreement does not survive correction. Agreement is thus confined to cells in which the
differences are small; no large image-removal difference is reproduced by any in-format probe. The in-format
probes also differ among themselves: on PathVQA, the black image separates MedGemma-4B from Gemma-3 by 19.2 points
while the two probes that change image \emph{content} show nothing, and at the question level the reliance labels
of image removal and a different image agree poorly ($\kappa$ from $-0.11$ to 0.23). A randomly chosen partner
image often has the same correct answer (all 23 chest X-ray partners that pose the same question), which
attenuates the different-image probe.

\paragraph{In-format probes on SLAKE.} The prediction that MedGemma-4B's answers would be \emph{more} stable than
Gemma-3's under a black image failed; the effect was in the opposite direction ($\kappa$ between answers with the
real and the black image: 0.11 \vs 0.33). On a black image, MedGemma-4B's yes-rate falls from 58\% to 28\%,
consistent with reading an empty image as an absence of findings, whereas Gemma-3's rises from 64\% to 84\%. On
SLAKE's opposite-answer pairs, MedGemma-4B follows the image in 72.8\% of cases and Gemma-3 in 24.8\%
(+48.0\ci{41.9}{53.8}, as predicted), and MedGemma-1.5 shows the same pattern (+36.5\ci{30.6}{42.1}). MedVLThinker
does not differ from its base under any in-format probe on any dataset, apart from a small black-image difference
on SLAKE ($-3.4$\ci{$-6.5$}{$-0.3$}). \Cref{sec:r4} tests whether the MedGemma advantage extends beyond SLAKE.

\subsection{What image removal responds to}
\label{sec:what}
\paragraph{Refusal.} The pre-registered format check ($m\ge0.9$) failed in a single condition, image removal. Free
generation shows why: ``\emph{Please provide the picture. I need to see the image to determine if there is a
spinal cord present}'' (Gemma-3). Without the image, Gemma-3 declines on 354 of the 1,206 questions, MedGemma-4B on
219 and MedGemma-1.5 on 8 (\cref{fig:abst}); MedVLThinker and Qwen2.5-VL never decline. On declined questions, the
forced answer is predominantly \emph{no} and unrelated to the model's answer with the image ($\kappa=-0.01$ for
Gemma-3, 0.04 for MedGemma-4B), so 53--55\% of these answers are classified as image-reliant. The largest
image-removal differences occur where refusal rates differ most: on VQA-RAD, Gemma-3 declines on half of the
questions, 23 points more often than MedGemma-4B and 48 points more often than MedGemma-1.5. When abstention is
permitted, MedGemma-4B declines on 93.0\% of questions and Gemma-3 on 99.7\% ($-6.7$, as predicted), eliminating
most of the 11.2-point difference observed under the forced format. For MedGemma-1.5, which almost never declines,
the \dang{} difference falls to +3.0\ci{$-3.6$}{9.5} on the 467 questions that both models answer.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig4_abstention.pdf}
\caption{Share of yes/no questions on which the model declines to answer when the image is removed ($m<0.5$;
95\% CIs from a bootstrap over images). Top: the main-run instruction (``Answer with only yes or no''). Bottom:
the instruction that permits ``unknown''.}
\label{fig:abst}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Agreement between prior and image.} Refusal does not account for all of the difference: on the 436
questions that both MedGemma-4B and Gemma-3 answer without the image ($m\ge0.9$), the \dang{} difference remains
+8.0\ci{2.9}{13.3}, and image removal still separates the two Qwen-based models, neither of which declines. When a
model's prior matches the image content, its answer is the same with and without the image, and image removal
classifies the answer as image-independent. MedGemma-4B's answers without the image exceed the majority-answer
prior on PathVQA, which it was not trained on (+5.0, \cref{tab:tests}; +11.9\ci{7.1}{16.6} among questions it
answers), and agree with its answers with the image beyond chance ($\kappa=0.21$ \vs 0.11 for Gemma-3). In the
Qwen pair, the base model's answers without the image agree more ($\kappa=0.16$ \vs 0.09), and image removal
correspondingly classifies the base model as less reliant.

\paragraph{What the \dang{} share contains.} Two decompositions show what MedGemma-4B's excess of 13.7 points is
made of. First, it consists of correct answers (\cref{fig:p3}, bottom): \dang{}-and-correct is 39.2\% \vs 25.1\%
(+14.1\ci{11.1}{17.1}), whereas \dang{}-and-incorrect, the category that would mislead a user, is 11.3\% \vs 11.7\%
($-0.4$\ci{$-2.7$}{2.0}). MedGemma-1.5's excess is likewise correct (+9.3 correct, +0.5 incorrect). Second, much of
any \dang{} share on yes/no questions is chance: an answer is classified as image-independent whenever the answer
without the image equals the answer with it. MedGemma-4B's answers are unchanged without the image in 58.6\% of
cases, against 49.1\% expected from its answer distributions alone (Gemma-3: 49.7\% \vs 45.7\%). Combined with
consistency, this yields a \textbf{chance floor of 41.5\% (MedGemma-4B) and 35.8\% (Gemma-3)}, against observed
\dang{} shares of 50.5\% and 36.8\%. Approximately 6 of the 13.7 points reflect the difference in floors, partly
because MedGemma-4B is more consistent (84.5\% \vs 78.4\%), a desirable property that the metric counts against
it. The chance-corrected difference is $\Delta\kappa=+0.112$\ci{0.044}{0.180}.

\subsection{What in-format probes respond to: held-out data}
\label{sec:r4}
Both MedGemma models were trained on SLAKE (the evaluated images are disjoint from its training split, but the
image distribution and question templates are shared), whereas MedVLThinker was not. Training exposure therefore
explains the SLAKE results as well as greater image reliance does. We registered a test that separates the two:
the opposite-answer probe for all five models on PathVQA, which was excluded from MedGemma's training
(\cref{tab:tests}, \cref{fig:contrast}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig9_contrast.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{Opposite-answer images inside and outside the medical models' training data.} Share of pairs on
which the model changes its answer (follows the image) and on which it is right on both images (pair accuracy),
for SLAKE (367 pairs) and held-out PathVQA (1,192 pairs); 95\% CIs from a bootstrap over images. Blue: the medical
model of each pair; orange: its general-purpose base. Pair accuracy is 0\% for a model that ignores the image and
25\% for uninformative image-dependent answers.}
\label{fig:contrast}
\end{figure*}

On PathVQA, MedGemma-4B does not differ from Gemma-3 (+0.8\ci{$-2.7$}{4.2}), MedGemma-1.5 follows the image
\emph{less} often ($-5.6$\ci{$-9.1$}{$-2.0$}, $p_{\text{Holm}}=0.003$), and MedVLThinker matches its base as
predicted. Resampling PathVQA's 154 question templates instead of images leads to the same conclusions. Under the
decision rule fixed before the run, the SLAKE difference is reported as possibly reflecting the training
distribution, and the claim of greater image reliance is withdrawn for MedGemma-1.5. Every model follows the
partner image in 43--49\% of the 1,192 pairs and answers both images correctly in 36--43\%, above both reference
points (0\% and 25\%): all five models use pathology images, to a similar and modest degree. The held-out test
cannot separate training exposure from a difference between domains. PathVQA is not, however, a domain new to
MedGemma: its training included 32.5 million histopathology patch--caption
pairs~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma}; only the PathVQA questions and images are held out. Despite this training,
the advantage seen on SLAKE does not appear. On PathVQA, only the black-image probe separates MedGemma-4B from
Gemma-3 (+19.2), consistent with its response to an empty image rather than with greater use of image content.

\paragraph{Is the opposite-answer probe more than accuracy?} Mostly not (\cref{tab:pair}). In nine of the ten
model~$\times$~dataset cells, pair accuracy lies 1--6 points below the product of the two single-image accuracies:
knowing how accurate a model is on a distribution predicts how often it follows an opposite-answer image there.
This is why the in-format advantage follows the training data. MedGemma-4B is 24 points more accurate than Gemma-3
on these SLAKE questions and about as accurate on PathVQA, and its advantage under the probe appears and
disappears accordingly. The exception is the informative case. Gemma-3 on SLAKE is right on 61.0\% of single images
but on both images of only 23.4\% of pairs, 13.8 points\ci{11.9}{15.6} below the product: it gives the same answer
to both images in 75.2\% of pairs, so 37.6 of its 61.0 accuracy points come from answers that do not depend on the
image. For MedGemma-4B, that part is 13.6 of 85.3. On these questions Gemma-3's accuracy overstates its use of the
image, which single-image accuracy cannot reveal and which the opposite-answer probe measures directly.

\subsection{Image reliance does not identify errors}
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig3_selective.pdf}
\caption{AUROC for ranking correct above incorrect yes/no answers (test split, 95\% CIs): the model's confidence
\vs label-free image reliance under each probe.}
\label{fig:sel}
\end{figure}

If image-independent answers were the unreliable ones, image reliance could serve as an error signal. Ranking
yes/no answers by image PMI separates correct from incorrect answers at chance level (\cref{fig:sel}; AUROC
\textbf{0.513}\ci{0.473}{0.552} for MedGemma-4B, 0.532 for Gemma-3), whereas the model's own confidence reaches
0.709 and 0.603 (higher by 0.197\ci{0.145}{0.250} and 0.071\ci{0.026}{0.116}). The degree to which an answer
depends on the image is thus not informative about its correctness.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
\paragraph{What image removal measures.} Removing the image poses a question about an image that is absent. The
response depends first on whether the model answers at all and on the quality of its priors, and only then on
whether it would have used the image. Across three model pairs and three datasets, image removal ranked the
medical model against its base differently from the in-format probes in six of nine cells, agreed with them only
where differences were small, and showed its largest differences where refusal differed most. The corroborating
checks of the original study (black image, random swaps) agreed with image removal on its chest X-ray
models~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent}; on our models and data they do not, in line with the conceptual argument
against removal for chest radiography~\cite{lotfinia2026cxr}. A \dang{} share is therefore underspecified without
its probe, and a comparison of \dang{} shares obtained by image removal may reflect refusal policy more than image
use.

\paragraph{What the in-format probes measure.} The in-format probes are not free of confounds either, and none of
them is a ground truth for the others. On SLAKE, they indicate that both MedGemma models rely on the image far more
than Gemma-3; on PathVQA, outside their training data, they do not. The opposite-answer probe, the only one with a
defined correct response, measures the \emph{correct} use of the image: pair accuracy is 83--99\% of the follow
rate for every model and set, and it stays close to what accuracy predicts. This has two consequences. First,
image reliance in this sense is a property of a model \emph{and} a data distribution, not of a model alone, so an
in-format probe evaluated on a model's training distribution reports what the model learned there. Second, a null
result on held-out data has two readings: on PathVQA every model is right on only 57--71\% of single images, and a
model cannot follow an image it cannot read, so equal results there may reflect equal difficulty as much as equal
reliance. What the probe adds to accuracy is the part of accuracy that is not earned from the image
(\cref{tab:pair}), which is the quantity a reliance audit is after. For the three pairs studied, no general claim
of greater image reliance by the medical model survives evaluation on held-out data.

\paragraph{Residual risk.} MedGemma-4B's additional \dang{} answers are correct, and the share of stable,
image-independent and incorrect answers is the same for both models. MedGemma-4B makes fewer errors overall (25.7\%
\vs 37.6\%), but a larger share of them fall into this category (44\% \vs 31\%, +12.9\ci{6.0}{19.9}); such errors
would not be detected by consistency or reliance checks.

\paragraph{Recommendations for reliance audits.} (1)~Do not rank models by image removal. Assess reliance with an
image that requires a different answer, and test the agreement between probes directly rather than comparing their
significance. (2)~Evaluate in-format probes on data outside each model's training set, and consult training
documentation before comparing models. (3)~Read pair accuracy against single-image accuracy, and report the share
of accuracy that comes from unchanged answers. (4)~Report the \dang{} share together with its chance floor, or as
$\kappa$, and decompose it by correctness; on balanced yes/no data, a model whose answers without the image are
pure noise is about 50\% ``not reliant''. (5)~Permit abstention, and treat declining without an image as
appropriate behavior rather than as a format failure.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
Three model pairs from two families establish that image removal \emph{can} rank models differently from in-format
probes and indicate why; they do not establish how often this occurs across models, and our claim is limited to
the models and data studied. No probe is a ground truth: the reference probe exists only on SLAKE and PathVQA, so
on VQA-RAD image removal is compared with two probes that are themselves weak, one attenuated and one not neutral.
The refusal and prior-agreement accounts, the per-dataset analysis (\cref{fig:bydataset}), the direct test of
disagreement (\cref{tab:did}) and the comparison of pair accuracy with accuracy (\cref{tab:pair}) were formulated
after the primary results; among the dataset-specific comparisons, only the held-out opposite-answer test was
registered. That test covers a single modality, pathology, on which all models perform modestly (pair accuracy
36--43\%); it argues against a general advantage but cannot exclude one in every domain, and it cannot distinguish
equal reliance from equal difficulty. The opposite-answer results on SLAKE rest on templated questions that recur
across images; resampling templates instead of images leaves the conclusions unchanged. MedGemma-4B was also
trained on VQA-RAD, nearly all of whose test images appear in its training split, so its VQA-RAD results may
reflect exposure; the training data of the general models are not published. A medical model and its base differ
in their entire post-training, not only in medical data. Refusal is inferred from first-token probability mass and
confirmed on a sample by free generation. All models answer in a forced format from the first token; MedVLThinker
was trained to reason before answering, so its results describe the model without its reasoning step. A single
instruction template was used, and refusal depends on the instruction. The opposite-answer pairs inherit the label
noise of their datasets (PathVQA's labels are generated automatically), which lowers attainable pair accuracy
equally for both models of a pair. Only open models of 3--4B parameters were studied; larger and proprietary models
may behave differently. Paraphrase equivalence was judged by an LLM and \textbf{was not validated by independent
human raters}; a check of 50 paraphrases, rated by the first author with AI assistance, accepted 88\% (above the
pre-specified 85\%) but is not independent of AI judgment. This is the principal limitation of the consistency
measure; the probe comparison does not use paraphrases. PathVQA questions are generated automatically and are often
ungrammatical. The chance correction and the correctness and refusal decompositions were introduced after the
results were known. Excluding the 330 pilot questions used to tune the design leaves every conclusion unchanged
(no-image accuracy above the prior on PathVQA +6.3\ci{2.4}{10.6}; \dang{} difference +12.9\ci{8.9}{17.1}).
Benchmark VQA is not clinical use, and we make no clinical claims.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
By the image-removal criterion, MedGemma-4B gives image-independent answers more often than its general-purpose
counterpart. Probes that keep an image in the input rank the same models differently, in most of the model pairs
and datasets we examined and by up to 60 points. Image removal responds to whether a model answers without an
image and to whether its priors agree with the image; probes that keep the image respond to how well a model reads
the evaluated distribution, and indicate greater reliance for the medical models only on data they were trained on.
Comparisons of image reliance between models therefore require images that call for a different answer, on
held-out data, read against accuracy, together with chance correction and a decomposition by correctness.

\appendix
\section{Implementation details}
\label{sec:impl}
\paragraph{Pipeline.} The experiments are implemented as a Python package (\texttt{medvlm}) with a command-line
interface: \texttt{prepare} (download, deterministic sampling, hash-verified images), \texttt{paraphrase}
(generation with rule-based and judgment-based validation, fail-closed), \texttt{pipeline} (resumable inference in
parts with checkpoint analysis), \texttt{probes} (black image, abstention permitted, opposite-answer image on SLAKE), \texttt{contrast}
(the held-out opposite-answer probe), and \texttt{analyze},
\texttt{compare}, \texttt{posthoc}, \texttt{replication} and \texttt{contamination}, which produce all tables and
figures in this paper. Configurations are layered by base, profile, model and hardware. Each job is a (question,
condition) pair keyed by identifier, so that interrupted runs resume without recomputation; every run records its
configuration, commit and library versions. Registrations are git tags.

\paragraph{Inference.} PyTorch 2.11 and Hugging Face Transformers 5.19, bf16, SDPA attention, one RTX 4080 SUPER
(16\,GB). MedGemma-4B requires 0.23\,s per call (18,896 calls in about 75 minutes, 8.2\,GB peak memory). During
pre-flight testing, we found that in bf16 the \emph{batch size} alone changes teacher-forced log-probabilities by up
to 1.09 nats (median 0.17) on identical, unpadded inputs, while $P(\text{yes})$ changes by at most 0.008. An fp32
output head did not remove the effect, which therefore originates inside the network. All runs consequently use
batch size 1, at a cost of about 1.5$\times$ in throughput. A regression check reproduced the pilot run, performed
on a T4, on the final GPU (98.5\% identical answers, mean $|\Delta P(\text{yes})|=0.004$).

\paragraph{Testing.} 104 unit tests and 7 tests with real models cover, among others, scoring edge cases, the
paraphrase rules (including every failure class found in the audit), batching equivalence, crash-safe resumption,
the coverage of the cluster bootstrap (by simulation), the test-split restriction of P3, the chance correction of
$\kappa$, the construction of opposite-answer partners, an oracle-\vs-blind check of pair accuracy, and the
difference-of-differences test of probe disagreement.

\section{Paraphrase equivalence rubric}
\label{app:rubric}
A pair is \textbf{accepted} only if both questions ask exactly the same thing, so that the correct answer cannot
differ. Permitted: perception framing (``can X be seen'', ``is X visible'', ``can X be seen to be enlarged''), exact
synonyms (clavicle/collarbone, encephalon/brain, intravenous contrast/dye), and reordering. \textbf{Rejected}: a
statement of fact turned into one of possibility or capability (``Is the heart enlarged?''$\to$``Can the heart be
enlarged?''); a broadened or narrowed term (mass$\to$lesion, organs$\to$structures, digestive system$\to$GI tract,
skull fracture$\to$cranial injury); a changed scope or presupposition (``Do the organs exist in X''$\to$``Are there
organs in X''); added qualifiers, findings or modalities (``bilaterally'', ``on imaging studies'',
``radiograph''); a reversed or altered relation (``does A show B''$\to$``is A associated with B'', ``mass lateral
to X''$\to$``X lateral to mass''); antonyms (healthy$\leftrightarrow$unhealthy, coronal$\to$transverse); two
questions in one; and malformed text. Rejections by class: relation 447, term 364, modality of statement 106,
added content 102, organ$\to$structure 47, generic collapse 30, polarity 19, scope 9 (plus rejections of the
template-based pass).

\section{Deviations from the pre-registration}
\label{app:dev}
All changes made after the analysis plan was fixed, with their rationale.

\smallskip\noindent\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.36\linewidth}p{0.6\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
Change & Rationale and effect\\
\midrule
Batch size 1 for all runs & bf16 batching shifts teacher-forced log-probabilities by up to 1.09 nats; decided before the main run.\\
Validator v2/v3, \emph{plain} style excluded, full equivalence screen, template styles & Audit acceptance below the pre-specified 85\% threshold; decided before the main run.\\
Format stopping rule triggered (image removal only) & Attributable to model behavior (refusal), not to a pipeline error; forced-choice $P(\text{yes})$ retained, refusal reported, P1 and P3 re-estimated without refusals.\\
P2 computed on the model's own answer $\hat y$ & The registered formula used the reference answer, which is unavailable at deployment and predicts correctness by construction.\\
P3 restricted to the test split & An analysis error had pooled the validation split; corrected to the registered set.\\
Chance correction; correctness and refusal decompositions; answer-change comparison across probes; per-dataset analysis & Added after the main run; descriptive, reported alongside the registered estimates.\\
Robustness probes R1--R3 & Registered after the main run and before being run (pre-registration \S15); R3 restricted to SLAKE as registered.\\
Additional pairs, H9--H11 & Registered before being run (\S16); all three new models passed the registered format check.\\
Probe R4, H12a--c & Registered before being run (\S17), following the training-data review; H12a not supported, H12b reversed; under the registered decision rule, the hypothesis that the MedGemma models rely on the image more was withdrawn.\\
Direct test of probe disagreement (\cref{tab:did}); pair accuracy against the accuracy product (\cref{tab:pair}) & Added after all results were known, from the stored outputs (\S19). They replace a count of significant cells as the summary of probe disagreement. Post hoc.\\
Training-data statements & Corrected after re-examining the documentation (\S18): MedGemma-4B was trained on VQA-RAD; the MedGemma-1.5 model card lists only SLAKE.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
